(CNN) -- While all eyes seem to be on "Slumdog Millionaire" for the Oscars, one very courageous little girl will be focused on another India-based film at the ceremony. Pinki, like millions in developing countries, had to live with her deformity and suffer the social consequences. "Smile Pinki" tells the story of her transformation from a sad outcast to a vibrant 8-year-old with plenty of spunk. Pinki was born with a cleft lip, and her impoverished family did not have the money for corrective surgery. Like millions of other children born with the lip deformity in developing countries, Pinki simply had to live with it and suffer the social consequences. Her father Rajendra Sonkar says: "She used to go to school and the kids would not befriend her. She would say, 'I don't want to go to school.'"  Watch how Pinki was transformed by the operation » . "Pinki was a depressed, sad, lonely, shy, young little girl, growing up on the periphery of the society in a little village," said Satish Kalra, director of Smile Train's South Asian region, after meeting with Pinki. The little girl's own family was ashamed of her, Kalra says. But all of that has changed. Pinki is now a real pistol, full of energy and confidence, and she has a fantastic smile too -- thanks to the Smile Train charity. Smile Train teaches doctors in their own countries to operate on cleft lips, a deformity afflicting up to four million children across the world. iReport: Share your Oscar predictions . Pinki just happened to be one of the chosen candidates for surgery and was also chosen to be the subject of the documentary. The film chronicles her transformation, following her from her village to the hospital and home again. "She has absolutely and totally changed," said Pinki's surgeon, Dr. Subodh Kumar. The film's director is Megan Mylan. She has won several awards but not an Oscar -- until now. For Pinki and her dad, being able to see the film's director win an Oscar would be a thrill. But they know they already have the greatest prize: Pinki's new smile. "I am so happy that my daughter's lips have been repaired," her dad Rajendra said with a smile, expressing hope that the movie will inspire people to help children whose families can't afford the surgery.

**Beyond the “Slumdog” Spotlight, a Smile Takes Center Stage**

On a night when the world’s cameras seemed trained on the cast and creators of *Slumdog Millionaire*, another Indian story quietly made its way down the Oscar red carpet — smaller, more intimate, but no less powerful.

Pinki Sonkar, a young girl from a poor village in Uttar Pradesh, arrived in Hollywood not as an actress, nor as a celebrity shaped by the film industry, but as the subject of a documentary about a life transformed by surgery most families like hers could never afford. The film, *Smile Pinki*, followed her journey from isolation to confidence after a free operation repaired her cleft lip.

While *Slumdog Millionaire* dominated headlines as the global success story of the season, *Smile Pinki* offered a different kind of triumph. It did not unfold in the crowded lanes of Mumbai or in the sweep of a fictional rags-to-riches narrative. Instead, it began in a rural community where a child’s untreated cleft lip had made her an object of stares, teasing and exclusion.

For Pinki, the condition was not simply medical. It shaped how others saw her and how she saw herself. Like many children born with cleft lips or palates in areas with limited access to health care, she faced social stigma as well as physical difficulty. Eating, speaking and attending school could become daily challenges. The cost of surgery placed treatment far beyond the reach of her family.

That changed when she was connected with doctors providing free cleft repair surgery through charitable medical outreach. The operation, relatively straightforward for trained surgeons, carried life-altering consequences. In *Smile Pinki*, the camera lingers not on spectacle but on the gradual return of possibility — a child stepping out from behind shame, learning to smile openly, and beginning to take her place among other children.

Her presence at the Academy Awards gave the film’s message a human face. Dressed for an occasion unimaginably distant from her village life, Pinki became a reminder that the Oscars are not only about glamour, box office success or celebrity. Sometimes they illuminate the quiet work of doctors, aid workers and families whose victories are measured not in ticket sales, but in restored dignity.

The contrast with *Slumdog Millionaire* was striking. Danny Boyle’s film became the evening’s sensation, celebrated for its energy, music and sweeping story of destiny. Its young stars drew international attention, and its wins were hailed as a landmark moment for Indian stories on the world stage. Yet amid that celebration, Pinki’s story cut through with a different emotional force: not the dream of winning a fortune, but the simple, profound gift of being able to smile without fear.

*Smile Pinki*, directed by Megan Mylan, won the Academy Award for Best Documentary Short Subject. Its victory brought attention to the millions of children worldwide living with untreated cleft conditions, many of whom can be helped through surgeries that take less than an hour but can transform an entire life.

For Pinki, the Oscar ceremony was a dazzling moment — lights, photographers, applause, and the strange wonder of being recognized in a place far from home. But the deeper significance of her journey lay elsewhere. It was in the schoolyard she could return to, the friendships she could form, the confidence she could carry, and the future that no longer had to be defined by a correctable condition.

In a year when India’s presence at the Oscars was largely framed through the exuberance of *Slumdog Millionaire*, Pinki Sonkar’s walk into the same spotlight told a quieter truth. Behind one child’s repaired smile was a story about access, compassion and the extraordinary impact of basic medical care.

Hollywood celebrated a film. Pinki carried something even more enduring back home: the chance to be seen, not for her cleft, but for herself.
